claims.claim: Hong Kong should tighten protection for tenants but not impose a hard rent cap.
Tenure security is a bigger problem than rent prices.
Blunt rent control rules carry real risks.
Mr Chan pays $5,800 in rent, about a third of his household income.
Mr Chan's worst problem is insecurity, not the rent price.
Mr Chan's last landlord ended the tenancy with two weeks' notice after he requested a repair.
A rent cap alone does not address tenants' insecurity.
Mr Chan says a hard cap could free up around $800 a month, about a month of food.
Mr Chan worries landlords would rather turn cubicles into storage than rent to regulated tenants.
Mr Chan has seen two units on his floor emptied and locked for a year.
Berlin capped rents on about 1.5 million flats in 2020.
After Berlin's cap, asking rents for new listings fell sharply.
The supply of listed flats in Berlin shrank within a year because owners held flats back or moved them to uncontrolled segments.
Losing supply in Hong Kong's already scarce subdivided unit market would hurt the intended beneficiaries.
Berlin's rent cap was struck down in 2021 for legal reasons about federal powers, not economics.
After Berlin's cap fell, suppressed increases returned and new contract rents jumped above the earlier trend.
A hard and temporary rent cap can leave tenants worse off than before.
Hong Kong should focus on security of tenure rather than a hard cap.
Longer notice periods and protection for tenants who request repairs are needed.
A softer limit on rent increases could accompany tenure protections to avoid landlords locking units away.
The argument is limited by relying on only two sources: one interview and one comparison with a very different city.
The author did not examine data or economic papers, so cannot estimate the supply effect in Hong Kong.

cites.sentence: He pays 5,800 dollars in rent, about a third of the household income [D3p1].
His last landlord ended the tenancy with two weeks notice after he asked for a leaking window to be repaired [D3p1].
He says a hard cap could free up around 800 dollars a month, which is about a month of food [D3p2].
Yet he worries that landlords would rather turn cubicles back into storage rooms than deal with regulated tenants, and he has seen two units on his floor emptied and locked for a year [D3p2].
But the supply of listed flats shrank within a year because owners held flats back or moved them into segments that were not controlled [D7p1].
The court struck the law down in 2021 for legal reasons about federal powers, not because of the economics [D7p2].
When the cap fell, suppressed increases came back and rents for new contracts jumped above the earlier trend [D7p2].
That means longer notice periods and protection for tenants who ask for repairs, which is exactly what Mr Chan said went wrong for him [D3p1].
A softer limit on rent increases could sit alongside this, so that landlords are not pushed to lock units away [D3p2].
